1.q: הֵ֥ן לְ⁠צֶ֖דֶק יִמְלָךְ מֶ֑לֶךְ וּ⁠לְ⁠שָׂרִ֖ים לְ⁠מִשְׁפָּ֥ט יָשֹֽׂרוּ
1.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Behold, a king and his princes will truly reign with righteousness and justice]

Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a righteous way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a just way]

2.q: וְ⁠הָיָה אִ֥ישׁ כְּ⁠מַֽחֲבֵא ר֖וּחַ וְ⁠סֵ֣תֶר זָ֑רֶם
2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a hiding place** protects a person from the wind and **a refuge** protects a person from the storm, so this ruler will protect his people from harm. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And a man will protect his people from harm, like a hiding place protects a person from the wind and provides a refuge from the storm]

The terms **a hiding place from the wind** and **a refuge from the storm** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [like a refuge from the wind and the storm]

The point of this comparison is that just as **streams of water in the desert** sustain and give life to everything around them, so this ruler will sustain and provide for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like streams of water that sustain life in the desert]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the shadow of a great rock** provides relief from the heat **in a weary land**, so this ruler will provide relief and comfort for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a great rock whose shadow gives relief to people in a dry and weary land]

3.note: Isaiah is using the **eyes** of these people to represent the people themselves in the act of **seeing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And those who see]

The phrase translated as **will not look away** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Scholars noted that with different vowels, it would say “will not be blinded,” which may fit the meaning of this passage better. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [will not be blinded]

If “will not look away” is the original reading, Isaiah is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression, **look away**, that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [And those who see will look intently]

Isaiah is using the **ears** of these people to represent the people themselves in the act of **hearing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who hear]

4.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the **heart** were the place where a person thinks and understands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the mind of the ones hastening themselves will understand knowledge]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is known]

Isaiah is using **the tongue** to represent the whole person in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the ones who stutter will hasten to speak clearly]

Isaiah is using the adjective **stuttering** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who cannot speak clearly]

5.note: The pronoun **It** does not refer to a specific person but is used as an impersonal subject. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [People will no longer call]

The expression **be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People will no longer call]

The expression **be said** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one will say]

6.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **folly**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [foolish words]

6.q: וְ⁠לִבּ֖⁠וֹ יַעֲשֶׂה־אָ֑וֶן לַ⁠עֲשׂ֣וֹת חֹ֗נֶף וּ⁠לְ⁠דַבֵּ֤ר אֶל־יְהוָה֙ תּוֹעָ֔ה לְ⁠הָרִיק֙ נֶ֣פֶשׁ רָעֵ֔ב וּ⁠מַשְׁקֶ֥ה צָמֵ֖א יַחְסִֽיר
6.note: Here, **to do** and **to speak** and **to make** mark the actions that follow as the goal or purpose of the fool’s speaking and doing **iniquity**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. See the UST.

Isaiah is speaking as if the **heart** were where a person’s intentions and desires exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he intends to do evil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [evil acts]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **godlessness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to act in ways that dishonor God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **error**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [untrue words]

Here, **the soul** represents the hungry person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to make the hungry person empty]

Isaiah is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to make those who are hungry stay empty]

Isaiah is using the adjective **thirsty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and he makes thirsty people go without drink]

7.note: The pronoun **He** refers to the scoundrel. The pronoun is repeated for emphasis. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [This scoundrel, he devises wicked plans]

Isaiah is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are poor]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with lying words]

Isaiah is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the needy person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is right]

Isaiah uses the word **though** here to indicate a contrast between the scoundrel’s wicked plans and the fact that the needy person speaks what is just. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [even though the needy speaks what is just]

8.note: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the noble person described in this verse and the scoundrel described in the previous verse. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [In contrast, a noble]

Isaiah is using the adjective **noble** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But a noble person]

The pronoun **he** refers to the noble person. It is repeated for emphasis. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and on noble things he, the noble person, will stand]

Isaiah is speaking as if the noble person could physically **stand** on noble things like on would stand on a foundation. This means that the noble person will persist in his commitment to what is noble. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will persist in noble things]

9.q: נָשִׁים֙ שַֽׁאֲנַנּ֔וֹת קֹ֖מְנָה שְׁמַ֣עְנָה קוֹלִ֑⁠י בָּנוֹת֙ בֹּֽטח֔וֹת הַאְזֵ֖נָּה אִמְרָתִֽ⁠י
9.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. See the UST.
Here, **my voice** represents what Isaiah is about to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [hear what I say]

Here, **my word** represents what Isaiah is about to say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [listen to what I am about to say]

10.q: יָמִים֙ עַל שָׁנָ֔ה תִּרְגַּ֖זְנָה בֹּֽטְח֑וֹת כִּ֚י כָּלָ֣ה בָצִ֔יר אֹ֖סֶף בְּלִ֥י יָבֽוֹא
10.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [In a year and a few days, those who are confident now will tremble, because there will be no grape harvest and no harvest of other crops]

11.note: Isaiah is using the adjective **haughty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [haughty women]

The terms **strip** and **bare** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [strip yourselves completely]

Isaiah assumes that readers will know that the instruction to **gird upon loins** means to wear sackcloth, the traditional symbol of repentance or grief. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [text] Alternate translation: [and gird sackcloth upon your loins]

Girding sackcloth upon the loins was a symbolic action by which people showed grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and tie sackcloth around your waists to show your grief]

12.note: Beating upon the breasts was a symbolic action by which people showed grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Show grief and mourning by beating your chests]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **delight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [delightful things]

13.note: The terms **thorn** and **briar** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [thorny weeds]

Isaiah says **all of the houses of rejoicing** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [even in every last house of rejoicing, that is, the exultant city]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [joyful celebration]

14.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The expression **will be abandoned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will stand empty]

The expression **will be forsaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone will forsake]

The terms **a delight of donkeys** and **a pasture of flocks** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [where wild donkeys and flocks of sheep will wander freely]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **delight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a place that donkeys delight in]

15.note: The word **until** indicates that the desolation described in the previous verses will continue up to the point when the Spirit comes. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [until the Spirit is poured on us from the height; when that happens,]

Isaiah is speaking as if the **Spirit** were a liquid that could be **poured** out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Spirit is given to us from the height]

The expression **is poured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh pours the Spirit on us]
The pronoun **us** refers to the people of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on the people of Judah]

Here, **the height** represents heaven, the place where God dwells. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from where God dwells on high]

The expression **is regarded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will regard agricultural land as a forest]

16.note: Isaiah is speaking of **justice** as if it were a living thing that could **stay** in a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And people will act with justice in the wilderness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just]

Isaiah is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were a living thing that could **dwell** in a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and people will do what is right in agricultural land]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and doing what is right]

17.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [doing what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [living peacefully]

17.q: וַֽ⁠עֲבֹדַת֙ הַ⁠צְּדָקָ֔ה הַשְׁקֵ֥ט וָ⁠בֶ֖טַח עַד עוֹלָֽם
17.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the service of righteousness will be quietness and confidence forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confidence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and feeling confident]

18.note: The pronoun **my** could refer to Yahweh, who is speaking through Isaiah, or to Isaiah himself identifying with his people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **habitation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in homes of]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in peaceful homes]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in secure residences]

19.q: וּ⁠בָרַ֖ד בְּ⁠רֶ֣דֶת הַ⁠יָּ֑עַר וּ⁠בַ⁠שִּׁפְלָ֖ה תִּשְׁפַּ֥ל הָ⁠עִֽיר
19.note: The word that the ULT translates as **when** indicates that the hailing and **the forest comes down** happen at the same time as the city becoming low. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [And it will hail at the same time the forest comes down, and in lowness the city will become low]

Isaiah is speaking as if the enemy nation were a **forest** that **comes down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when the enemy nation falls]

Isaiah is speaking as if the humiliation and defeat of the enemy city were a physical **lowness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the city will be humiliated and defeated]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the word **low** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and the city will be utterly laid low]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lowness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in humiliation]

20.q: אַשְׁרֵי⁠כֶ֕ם זֹרְעֵ֖י עַל כָּל מָ֑יִם מְשַׁלְּחֵ֥י רֶֽגֶל הַ⁠שּׁ֖וֹר וְ⁠הַ⁠חֲמֽוֹר
20.note: Isaiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of blessing and well-being. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How blessed you will be, you who sow beside all waters, you who let the ox and the donkey roam freely]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **happiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How happy you are,]

Isaiah says **beside all waters** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [beside many sources of water]

Isaiah is using **senders of the foot of the ox and the donkey** as a common expression of the culture to mean “letting their livestock graze freely.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who let their livestock graze freely]
